'''writing-book''' (rī′ting-bu̇k), ''n.'' A blank book for practice in penmanship; a copy-book.

'''writing-box''' (rī′ting-boks), ''n.'' A small box containing a set of the materials used in Chinese or Japanese writing. See ''writing-set'', 2.

'''writing-cabinet''' (rī′ting-kab″i-net), ''n.'' A piece of furniture in which a writing-desk is combined with drawers or cupboards, shelves for books, or other appliances.

'''writing-case''' (rī′ting-kās), ''n.'' A case containing materials and affording facilities for writing; a kind of portable writing-desk.

'''writing-chambers''' (rī′ting-chām″bėrz), ''n. pl.'' Rooms or offices occupied by a lawyer and his clerks, etc.; a law office.

'''writing-desk''' (rī′ting-desk), ''n.'' '''1.''' A writing-table, especially one in which the whole or a part of the top is sloping, and the space below the top is occupied with drawers, pigeonholes, or shelves: sometimes there is also a raised frame or case of drawers, shelves, or pigeonholes. Compare ''writing-table'' and ''escritoire''.—'''2.''' A portable writing-case, usually made of

blotting-paper within it, which serve as a pad for writing on.

'''writing-frame''' (rī′ting-frām), ''n.'' A frame for the use of blind or partially blind persons in writing, made to hold the sheet of paper firmly, and furnished with an adjustable guide for the formation of lines.

'''writing-ink''' (rī′ting-ingk), ''n.'' See ''ink''<sup>1</sup>, 1.

'''writing-machine''' (rī′ting-mạ-shēn″), ''n.'' A typewriter.

'''writing-master''' (rī′ting-mȧs″tėr), ''n.'' '''1.''' One who teaches the art of penmanship.—'''2.''' The yellow bunting, ''Emberiza citrinella:'' so named from the irregularly scribbled lines on its eggs. Also called ''scribbling'' or ''writing lark'', for the same reason. See cut under ''yellowhammer''. [Local, Eng.]

'''writing-paper''' (rī′ting-pā″pėr), ''n.'' Paper finished with a smooth surface, generally sized, for writing on.

'''writing-reed''' (rī′ting-rēd), ''n.'' See ''reed''<sup>1</sup>.

'''writing-school''' (rī′ting-sköl), ''n.'' A school or an academy where handwriting or calligraphy is taught.

'''writhen†''' (riᴛ̵ʜ′en), ''p. a.'' Obsolete or archaic past participle of ''writhe.''

'''writheneck''' (riᴛ̵ʜ′nek), ''n.'' Same as ''wryneck'', 3.

'''writhingly''' (rī′ᴛ̵ʜing-li), ''adv.'' In a writhing manner; with writhing. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|“Oh!” turning over ''writhingly'' in her chair.
{{right|''R. Broughton'', Belinda, xxx.}}}}

'''writhle†''', ''v. t.'' See ''writhel.''

'''writing''' (rī′ting), ''n.''   [< ME. ''writing'', ''writunge'' (cf. Icel. ''ritning''); verbal n. of ''write'', ''v.'']   '''1.''' The recording of words or sounds in significant characters; in the most general sense, any use of or method of using letters or other conventional symbols of uttered sounds for the visible preservation or transmission of ideas; specifically, as distinguished from printing, stamping, incision, etc., the act or art of tracing graphic signs by hand on paper, parchment, or any other material, with a pen and ink, style, pencil, or any other instrument; also, the written characters or words; handwriting; chirography.
{{smaller block|We have, thus, in this inscription at Abou-Symbul a cardinal example of Greek ''writing'' as it was used by the Ionian and Dorian settlers in Asia Minor and the islands about the beginning of the sixth century {{sc|b. c.}}
{{right|''C. T. Newton'', Art and Archæol., p. 101.}}}}
{{smaller block|Roman ''writing''—capital, uncial, half-uncial, and cursive—became known to the Western nations, and in different ways played the principal part in the formation of the national styles of ''writing.'' {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XVIII. 155.}}}}
'''2.''' The state of being written; recorded form or expression: as, to put a proposition in ''writing''; to commit one’s thoughts to ''writing''. {{smaller|In law the expressions ''in writing'' and ''written'' are often construed to include printed matter as well as manuscript.}}

{{smaller block|Ther [in Candia] was lawe fyrst put in ''wrytyng.''
{{right|''Torkington'', Diarie of Eng. Travell, p. 19.}}}}
{{smaller block|Then Huram the king of Tyre answered in ''writing.''
{{right|2 Chron. ii. 11.}}}}

'''3.''' That which is written, or in a written state; a record made by hand in any way; a paper or instrument wholly or partly in manuscript; an inscription.

{{smaller block|The ''writing'' was the ''writing'' of God, graven upon the tables.
{{right|Ex. xxxii. 16.}}}}
{{smaller block|Whosoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a ''writing'' of divorcement.
{{right|Mat. v. 31.}}}}
{{smaller block|I accepted of the Offer, and ''Writings'' were immediately drawn between us.
{{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, I. 513.}}}}

'''4.''' A production of the pen in general; a literary or other composition; any expression of thought in visible words; a scripture.

{{smaller block|I know not whether it cause greater pleasure to reade their ''writings'', or astonishment and wonder at the Nation.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 176.}}}}
{{smaller block|The later Greek and Latin ''writings'' occasionally contain maxims [concerning war] which exhibit a considerable progress in this sphere.
{{right|''Lecky'', Europ. Morals, II. 273.}}}}

'''5.''' The expression of thought by written words; the use of the pen in conveying ideas; literary production.

{{smaller block|It is to the credit of that age [eighteenth century] to have kept alive the wholesome tradition that ''Writing'', whether in prose or verse, was an Art that required training at least, if nothing more. {{right|''Lowell'', New Princeton Rev., II. 156.}}}}

These objects are often made to correspond in material and design.—'''2.''' A set of the boxes, ink-stone, water-pot, etc., used in Chinese and Japanese writing, often of lacquer, or mounted in metal.

'''writing-table''' (rī′ting-tā″bl), ''n.'' '''1.''' A table fitted for writing upon, sometimes differentiated from a writing-desk, as being a piece of furniture for the library rather than for the business office.—'''2†.''' A tablet; a table-book.
{{smaller block|He asked for a ''writing-table'', and wrote, saying, His name is John.
{{right|Luke i. 63.}}}}
{{smaller block|The author defies them and their ''writing-tables''.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man out of his Humour, ii. 2.}}}}

{{smaller|'''Knee-hole writing-table''', a writing-table having a square or arched opening by which the knees of the person using it are accommodated under the surface upon which he writes, but with drawers, closets with pigeon-holes, or shelves, etc., on one or both sides. Also ''knee-hole desk''.}}

Not right in state, adjustment, or the like; ot in order; disordered; perverse; being awry amiss.
{{smaller block|I’ve heerd my aunt say as she found out as summat was ''rong'' wi’ Nancy as soon as th’ milk turned bingy.
{{right|''Mrs. Gaskell'', Sylvia’s Lovers, xv.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>For modes of faith let graceless zealots fight,
His can’t be ''wrong'' whose life is in the right.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Man, iii. 306.}}}}
{{smaller block|It is a ''wrong'', egotistical, savage, unchristian feeling, and that ’s the truth of it. {{right|''Thackeray'', Waterloo.}}}}
{{smaller block|Men’s judgments as to what is right and ''wrong'' are not perfectly uniform.
{{right|''J. Sully'', Outlines of Psychol., p. 558.}}}}
'''4.''' Deviating from that which is correct, proper, or suitable; not according to intention, requirement, purpose, or desire: as, the ''wrong'' side of a piece of cloth (the side to be turned inward).
{{smaller block|<poem>He call’d me sot,
And told me I had turn’d the ''wrong'' side out.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, iv. 2. 8.}}}}
{{smaller block|I observe the Moral is vitious; It points the ''wrong'' way, and puts the Prize into the ''wrong'' Hand.
{{right|''Jeremy Collier'', Short View (ed. 1698), p. 210.}}}}
{{smaller block|I swear she ’s no chicken; she ’s on the ''wrong'' side of thirty, if she be a day.
{{right|''Swift'', Polite Conversation, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|Were their faces set in the right or in the ''wrong'' direction?
{{right|''Macaulay'', Sir J. Mackintosh.}}}}
'''5.''' In a state of misconception or error; not correct in action, belief, assertion, or the like; mistaken; in error.
{{smaller block|<poem>I was ''wrong'',
I am always bound to you, but you are free.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Enoch Arden.}}}}
{{smaller block|You are ''wrong'', sir; you are ''wrong''. I have quite done with you. Be under no mistake upon that point.
{{right|''W. Besant'', St. Katharine’s, ii. 28.}}}}
{{smaller block|''Wrong'' is in all senses the opposite and correlative of ''right''. '''n the wrong box.''' See ''box''<sup>2</sup>.—'''Wrong font,''' said of a rinters’ type, etc., that is not of the proper size or face or its position. Abbreviated ''w. f.'' ='''Syn. 2.''' Unfit, unuitable, inappropriate, inapposite.—'''3.''' Immoral, inequitble, unfair.—'''4.''' Incorrect, faulty.}}

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' That which is wrong, amiss, or eroneous; the opposite of right, or of propriety, ruth, justice, or goodness; wrongfulness; eror; evil.
{{smaller block|<poem>And the abusyng of ȝour Offyce, . . .
And ȝour fals glosing of the ''wrang,''
Sall nocht mak ȝow to rax heir lang.</poem>
{{right|''Lauder'', Dewtie of Kyngis (E. E. T. S.), l. 131.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>A free determination
’Twixt right and ''wrong.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. and C., ii. 2. 171.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The weak, against the sons of spoil and ''wrong,''
Banded, and watched their hamlets, and grew strong.</poem>
{{right|''Bryant'', The Ages, st. 11.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Those who think to better ''wrong''
By working ''wrong'' shall seek thee wide
To slay thee.</poem>
{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, III. 34.}}}}

. Wrong action or conduct; anything done ntrary to right or justice; a violation of law, oligation, or propriety; in ''law'', an invasion of ght, to the damage of another person; a tort: , to do or commit ''wrong'', or a ''wrong''.
{{smaller block|For that Percevale ly Galoys was accused with grete ''ronge'' for the deth of the same hoot, like as an Ermyte t tolde after that hadde seyn all the dede.
{{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 475.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Cease your open ''wrongs!''
annot our Bishops scape your slanderous tongues?</poem>
{{right|''Times’ Whistle'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 10.}}}}
{{smaller block|t is probable that a man never knows the deep anguish conscious ''wrong'' until he has had the courage to face solitude its naked hideousness.
{{right|''J. Sully,'' Sensation and Intuition, p. 154.}}}}

Harm or evil inflicted; damage or detriment ffered; an injury, mischief, hurt, or pain imrted or received: as, to do one a ''wrong''.
{{smaller block|<poem>To forgive ''wrongs'' darker than death or night.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley,'' Prometheus, iv.}}}}

A state of being wrong or of acting wrongly; erroneous or unjust view, attitude, or prolure in regard to anything: chiefly in the rase ''in the wrong''.
{{smaller block|hey were neither of them dissatisfied with the knight’s ermination, because neither of them found himself ''in wrong'' by it.
{{right|''Addison,'' Spectator, No. 122.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>When People once are ''in the wrong,''
Each Line they add is much too long.</poem>
{{right|''Prior,'' Alma, iii.}}}}
{{smaller block|is I who ought to be angry and unforgiving; for I ''in the wrong.''
{{right|''Thackeray,'' De Finibus.}}}}

{{smaller|'''ndonment for wrongs.''' See ''abandonment.''—'''In wrong.''' See def. 4.—'''Private wrong.''' See ''private.''—'''o have wrong.''' (''a''†) To have or be on the wrong side; rong, or in the wrong.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>When I ''had wrong'' and she the right,
She wolde alwey so goodely
Forgeve me so debonairly.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer,'' Death of Blanche, l. 1282.}}}}
{{smaller|o suffer the infliction of wrong; have wrong treatt.}}

{{right|''Shak.,'' J. C., iii. 2. 115.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
